IB Computer Science

B4.1 Fundamentals of ADTs HL

Topic B4: Abstract Data Types | Structure = Speed

The Big Question HL

🤔 How can a website find a username in a database of millions…

in a fraction of a second?

❌ Common misconception: “It’s just faster computers.”

Hardware helps, but data structure choices often matter more.

✅ Reality: the right abstract data type can reduce work from O(n) to O(1) or O(log n).

That’s the difference between “scan everything” and “jump straight to it”.

HL What is an ADT?

Why describe “what it does” separately from “how it’s built”?

An ADT is defined by its interface (operations).

You can change the implementation without changing how users interact with it.

This is abstraction.

Example

A “set” ADT supports add, remove, contains…

It could be implemented using a hash table or a balanced tree.

🔗 Connection to B2.4: we compare implementations using Big O.

HL Choosing a data structure

What operations matter most for your problem?

Different structures optimize different operations (search, insert, delete, traversal).

You often trade time for space (or vice versa).

Worst-case vs average-case can differ (especially with hash tables).

Exam skill: justify a choice using operation needs + complexity.

HL Linked lists

What if you need a structure that can grow and shrink efficiently?

A linked list is made of nodes connected by pointers.

The head points to the first node; the tail ends the chain.

Deep Dive: singly, doubly, circular

Singly linked list

Each node stores data + a pointer to the next node.

Traversal is one direction only.

Doubly linked list

Nodes have next and previous pointers.

Faster navigation backwards, but uses more memory.

Circular linked list

Tail points back to head → continuous traversal.

Useful for round-robin scheduling patterns.

HL Linked list operations

Why can linked lists be efficient for inserts but slow for searching?

Traversal/search follows pointers node-by-node → often O(n).

Insertion (with the right pointer) can be O(1).

Deletion can also be O(1) once you locate the node.

Key idea

Lists don’t have random access like arrays (arr[i]).

You must traverse to reach the i-th element.

🧠 Quick Check HL

Explain one situation where a linked list is a better choice than an array.

Then state one disadvantage of linked lists.

Good use: lots of insertions/deletions in the middle (no shifting elements).

Disadvantage: slow random access/search (often O(n)) and extra memory for pointers.

HL Binary search trees (BSTs)

How can a tree make searching faster than scanning a list?

A BST stores values so that:

Left subtree < node < Right subtree

Search compares and moves left/right.

Terminology

root, parent, child, leaf, subtree

Complexity: balanced BST operations are often O(log n); unbalanced trees can degrade toward O(n).

HL BST operations

What operations should you be able to describe?

Insertion: compare and move left/right until a free leaf position.

Search: compare key with node, then move left/right.

Traversal: visiting nodes (e.g., in-order gives sorted order in a BST).

Deletion: cases depend on node children (0, 1, or 2 children).

🔗 Connection to A3: tree-based indexes can speed up database searching.

HL Sets as an ADT

What makes a set different from a list?

A set contains unique elements (no duplicates).

Order is not the focus; membership is.

Common operations: contains, add, remove.

Set operations

Union, intersection, difference, subset

🧠 Quick Check HL

Let A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {3, 4}.

State A ∪ B, A ∩ B, and A − B.

A ∪ B: {1, 2, 3, 4}

A ∩ B: {3}

A − B: {1, 2}

HL Hash tables

How can we look up values without searching through everything?

A hash table maps a key to an index using a hash function.

Average-case search/insert/delete can be near O(1).

Example

Key: "name" → hash → index → stored value

Used in dictionaries/maps, caches, and many database internals.

HL Collisions, load factor & rehashing

What if two different keys map to the same index?

Collision → needs a resolution strategy.

Load factor increases as the table fills → more collisions.

Rehashing increases table size and redistributes items.

Two collision strategies

Chaining (store a list at each index)

Open addressing (probe for another slot)

Trade-off

High load factor → slower operations; rehashing costs time but restores performance.

Misconception Check HL

True or False: “Hash table operations are always O(1).”

False. Collisions and high load factors can degrade performance; worst-case can approach O(n).

That’s why good hash functions, resizing/rehashing, and collision strategies matter.

Key Takeaways HL

  • An ADT is defined by operations; implementations can vary (abstraction).
  • Linked lists enable efficient inserts/deletes but searching is often O(n).
  • BSTs can support O(log n) operations when balanced; unbalanced trees can degrade.
  • Sets store unique values and support union/intersection/difference operations.
  • Hash tables offer fast average lookup, but collisions/load factor affect performance.

Connections: A3 uses indexes/hashing internally; B2 uses simpler structures (stacks/queues); A4 uses hashing in data workflows.
